title: Nunn Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Nunn wells have a 360-foot median depth, with typical finished-well costs of $18,600-$31,800.
h1: What Nunn, Colorado Wells Are Really Like
intro_html:
Buying land near Nunn means planning around a private well, not a municipal water connection. Permit records within 5 miles show a plains setting where wells commonly reach sedimentary rock or an unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifer. The practical questions are how deep the hole may be, how much water it can produce, what the finished system costs, and what nearby records say about the area.

The records include permitted wells in Weld County, with construction and water-level information available for only part of the total set. Use these figures to budget and compare parcels, then confirm the specific lot with a Colorado water-well contractor and the Colorado Division of Water Resources.

sections.heading: Nunn wells commonly reach the deeper plains sediments
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Nunn is 360 feet. The middle half runs from 200 to 480 feet, so a driller bidding a new well should not assume a shallow hole just because the property is on open plains. The 90th-percentile depth is 660 feet, and the deepest record reaches 900 feet.

Nearly half of the wells, 49%, fall between 300 and 600 feet. Another 16% are 600 feet or deeper, while 20% are under 100 feet and 15% are between 100 and 300 feet. Most named permits use an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, with some in the Laramie Fox Hills and Quaternary Alluvium. Local geology can change quickly from one parcel to the next.

sections.heading: Most Nunn wells make a usable household supply
sections.html:
Among the wells reporting pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute. The middle half produces 9.0 to 14.0 gallons per minute, and 78% report between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. That is a stronger production pattern than a buyer sees in many uncertain bedrock settings, but it is still not a guarantee for an untested parcel.

Another 21% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Only 1% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, and 0% are reported under 1 gallon per minute. The records are dominated by domestic or household permits, with stock use also common. Ask for the well completion report, pump test, storage setup, and permitted use before relying on a neighbor's yield.

sections.heading: The reported Nunn water level is holding steady
sections.html:
Reported static water levels have a median depth of 100 feet below the surface. The middle half ranges from 49 to 144 feet. That range matters when pricing a pump, because pumping equipment and electrical requirements depend partly on the lift from the water level to the pressure system.

The decade comparison does not show a measurable change in the median: the 2010s median is 100 feet and the 2020s median is also 100 feet. That is not proof that every well has a stable water level. It is a broad permit-record signal, and individual wells can respond differently to pumping, recharge, construction, and local geology. A current static measurement is more useful for a specific property.

sections.heading: Nunn has a long permit history and several repeat drillers
sections.html:
Permit activity is established in the Nunn area. The records show 6 permits in the 1950s, 14 in the 1960s, 33 in the 1970s, 36 in the 1980s, 76 in the 1990s, 220 in the 2000s, 154 in the 2010s, and 191 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025. There are 811 wells in the mapped record, although only 522 are recorded as constructed.

The most active names are Crandall Drilling & Pump Service, including Crandall Jr. and Howard H., with 188 records; Ingram Drilling Inc., including Ingram and Stephen E., with 96; and Lesh Drilling Inc., including Lesh Jr. and Ed, with 59. Those records identify local experience, not a guarantee of current availability or price.

sections.heading: Budget roughly $18,600 to $31,800 for a finished median-depth well
sections.html:
For Nunn's alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the drilling model uses a typical rate of $35 to $55 per foot. At the 360-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $12,600 to $19,800. That is only the hole, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $18,600 to $31,800 at that same median depth. A shallow or productive site may cost less, while a deeper hole, difficult access, casing and grout requirements, or a difficult pump installation can raise the bid. Request an itemized proposal that separates drilling, casing, grouting, testing, pump equipment, trenching, electrical work, and permit-related work.

sections.heading: Check water quality, septic setbacks, and building feasibility
sections.html:
Low yield is not the main warning signal in these records, but a good area statistic cannot rule out a poor individual well or a dry hole. Fractured-bedrock production is especially variable, and an unnamed aquifer label does not replace a site-specific evaluation. Confirm casing, grout, well construction, pump performance, and laboratory water testing.

Environmental screening also deserves attention. The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 33 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. There are 0 historic mine features in that area. These locations do not automatically make a parcel unsafe, but they justify checking the parcel's history, groundwater direction, and test results. Septic soil conditions, replacement-area requirements, driveway access, and the building envelope should be reviewed together with the well location.

sections.heading: Compare the lot's neighbors before you commit
sections.html:
Start with the Colorado DWR permit file for the parcel and nearby wells, then compare reported depths, yields, static water levels, aquifer descriptions, and permitted uses. Neighboring records in Pierce, Carr, Ault, Wellington, Eaton, and Severance can provide broader context, but the closest wells are usually the most useful comparison.

For an existing home, ask for the well permit, construction report, recent production information, water test, pump age, and records of repairs. For vacant land, obtain a drilling estimate based on the proposed well location and access route rather than relying only on the area median. Also confirm that the intended household, stock, irrigation, or other use is allowed. If the basin is over-appropriated, an augmentation plan may be necessary for some uses. Have the well, septic system, driveway, and house site reviewed as one project.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Nunn, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Nunn is 360 feet. The middle half runs from 200 to 480 feet. About 49% are between 300 and 600 feet, while 16% reach 600 feet or more. The deepest record is 900 feet, so a buyer should price the project around the property’s nearby well records rather than assume a shallow hole.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Nunn?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the 360-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $12,600 to $19,800. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $18,600 to $31,800. Actual bids depend on depth, access, casing and grout, pump equipment, and site conditions.

faq.q: How much water do Nunn wells produce?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a 10.0-gallon-per-minute median, with the middle half between 9.0 and 14.0 gallons per minute. About 78% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, while 21% report more than 15. The record shows 1% between 1 and 5 gallons per minute and 0% under 1, but nearby results do not guarantee a new well.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Nunn, Colorado?
faq.a: Permit records do not prove that a particular well is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles, the mapped record includes 33 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the actual well through a qualified laboratory, review the parcel and groundwater history, and retest when conditions or ownership change. Treatment should be based on test results.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near Nunn?
faq.a: The broad permit-record comparison does not show a change in the median reported static water level. It is 100 feet below surface in both the 2010s and the 2020s. The overall median is also 100 feet, with the middle half from 49 to 144 feet. That pattern does not guarantee stability for an individual well, so obtain a current static measurement when evaluating a property.
